name: Nora Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Nora. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Owen Pryce at Upper Banks, which is a hill farm, seventy suckler cows, that's beef cows rearing their own calves, plus hay and a bit of oats on the lower ground. In winter the cattle are in the shed, so my day is feeding silage, bedding them down with straw, and checking for anything off. Owen's sixty-six and a widower, and he does the thinking while I do the lifting. I've been there two years and I still get the mix wrong on the feeder wagon now and then.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's quiet and I know where I am with it. Cattle don't care what you look like or what you said on the internet. Luc, my partner, drives a milk tanker, so we're both up at silly hours and it suits us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask a few questions about each one. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing, probably. I don't really post anything, and at work it's just me and Owen and he only talks about the weather and the price of calves. If someone in the pub brought it up, I'd say I never thought it would amount to much on a hill farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief, I'll admit that. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't want to. If it stays as something office people use, that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Feed the cattle, get the hay in, put a bit by, we've got about four months' worth. Maybe ask Owen if I can have a go at the calving next spring instead of just watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you tried the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't see what they'd do for me. Luc showed me one on his phone, he asked it how to fix the tap, and it gave him a long answer that was wrong. I'd rather ask Owen. He's wrong sometimes too, but at least I can see his face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make next spring a good one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every calf alive and Owen trusting me with a heifer on my own. Last year I called him out at three in the morning for one that was fine. He wasn't cross, but I was.

S0.say: I'd mostly say nothing, since I don't post and work is just me and my boss. In the pub I'd say I never thought it would amount to much on a hill farm.
S0.think: Privately it would be a relief, because I've never used AI tools and don't want to. If it stays something office people use, that suits me.
S0.do: Keeps feeding cattle and making hay on the hill farm and keeps saving a little on top of four months' cushion. Asks her boss to let her handle calving herself next spring.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's the world she already knows.
S0.quote: I'd rather ask Owen. He's wrong sometimes too, but at least I can see his face.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is quiet, practical and wary of anything she can't see working. Her goals are concrete and small: handling calving without calling her boss. The story of the wrong tap advice shows how one bad experience settled her view of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably fair enough for big flat farms, and it'll take a while to reach places like ours. Some jobs go, some come, it's always been like that. I wouldn't get worked up about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be watching Owen's money. He's not the type to buy a robot, he still uses a diary from the feed merchant. But if he retires and the farm gets sold to someone with a bigger operation, they might not need me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd carry on and keep my head down. I'd save a bit more, maybe stop the Friday chippy. I wouldn't go chasing courses unless Owen asked me to, because I don't see the point of learning a machine that hasn't turned up yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like a noise in the engine you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Luc's job, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one that'd worry me more, if I'm honest. Self-driving lorries are already being tested, Luc's read about it. If they can drive a tanker up our lane in the snow, I'll eat my hat, but on the main roads, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Is that what you'd tell a younger worker too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'd tell a young lad to learn the new stuff. I just know I won't, and I'm not going to lie to you about it.

S1.say: I'd say it's fair enough for big flat farms and will take a while to reach hill farms, since some jobs go and some come. I wouldn't get worked up about it in public.
S1.think: I'd worry less about a robot than about my boss retiring and the farm being sold to a bigger operation that wouldn't need me. My partner's lorry job worries me more than mine.
S1.do: Carries on at the hill farm, saves a little more and drops the Friday takeaway. Avoids courses unless her boss asks, since she won't learn a machine before it arrives.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, like an engine noise she can't place.
S1.quote: I'd tell a young lad to learn the new stuff. I just know I won't, and I'm not going to lie to you about it.
S1.fieldNote: Nora's real worry is not the robot but her boss retiring and the farm changing hands. She admits openly that she would give others advice she won't follow herself. Her centre outlook shows as a shrug about jobs coming and going rather than blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three pictures all end in the same place. They differ in how much warning there is. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort out some kind of support quickly, because it's not people's fault. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign things. I'd say it to my mum and the neighbours, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years and both of us could be done. A robot tanker and a robot feeder, and Luc and I are sat at the kitchen table with four months of money and no idea what to do next. I'm not quick at new things. I'd be the one still looking when the jobs have all gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away: the second car, the phone contract, the holiday fund. I'd ask my brother Remy if there's any work at his garage, even sweeping up, and look at anything going in care or cleaning nearby. If it all went, we'd move back near my mum's and lean on family until something turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like when you find a dead calf in the morning and you know you missed something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luc that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing much. We're not big talkers. I'd put the kettle on and we'd sit there, and at some point one of us would say, well, we've done harder. I'm not sure we have, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Owen keep you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it were up to him, maybe for a bit, out of habit. But he's sixty-six. If a machine does it cheaper, his daughter in town would tell him to sell up or buy one. I'd not blame her, it's business.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to put support in place fast, because it isn't people's fault. I'd sign petitions rather than protest, and talk about it with my mum and the neighbours.
S2.think: Two years and both my partner's tanker job and my farm job could be gone, leaving us with four months of money. I'm slow with new things, so I'd be the one still looking when the jobs have gone.
S2.do: Cuts the second car, phone contract and holiday fund straight away and asks her brother about work at his garage while looking at local care or cleaning jobs. Moves back near her mother and leans on family if everything goes.
S2.feel: Sick with worry, like finding a dead calf and knowing she missed something.
S2.quote: Like when you find a dead calf in the morning and you know you missed something.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture hits Nora hard because both incomes in her household are exposed to robots. She doesn't blame anyone, not even the boss's daughter, and calls it business. Her plan is cutting costs and leaning on family, not reinventing herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, with five years' warning. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should have time to sort themselves out, and the government should help those who can't. I'd probably say it a bit more calmly than the two-year one, because five years feels like there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd waste most of it. I'd tell myself it's not here yet and carry on feeding cattle. Then in year four I'd be in a panic like the two-year one, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more away each month, aim for six months instead of four, and stop buying anything big. Luc's talked about doing a forklift ticket, so maybe I'd do one with him, it's cheap and it's a day. Mostly I'd wait and watch what happens to the bigger farms down the valley before I did anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's there every time I see something new on Owen's phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You think you'd waste the time. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone gave me a date. Owen saying, Nora, I'm selling in two years, would do more than any news story. I work better with a deadline than a warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a forklift ticket, if robots can do that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, they probably can. I suppose it's because it's something I know I can do. It's not a plan, it's more something to hold on to.

S3.say: I'd say people should have time to sort themselves out and the government should help those who can't. I'd say it more calmly than with two years, because five years feels like time.
S3.think: I think I'd waste most of the five years, telling myself it's not here yet, and then panic in year four. I work better with a deadline than a warning.
S3.do: Raises her savings target from four to six months and stops big purchases. Considers a one-day forklift ticket with her partner, but mostly watches the bigger farms down the valley before acting.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the worry surfacing whenever she sees something new.
S3.quote: It's not a plan, it's more something to hold on to.
S3.fieldNote: Nora predicted her own procrastination with real honesty. When I pointed out that robots could also drive forklifts, she accepted it and called the ticket something to hold on to. A concrete date from her boss would move her more than any warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, with the most time. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty of time for the country to make a plan. I'd hope they'd get on with it. I'm not going to march about something ten years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Owen will have retired by then anyway, so my job was always going to change. What worries me is being thirty-seven with no real trade, and Luc too. It's not the robot, it's that I never got good at anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working Upper Banks as long as Owen's there and keep saving. Luc and I were going to look at a mortgage next year, and I think we'd hold off and keep renting, because a mortgage on two jobs that might go isn't clever. I'd probably not do much else until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow way. The kind that sits there under everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Holding off the mortgage is a big decision. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luc wants a house with a bit of land, for a few sheep. I'd say let's wait two years and see. He'd say we said that last year. He'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never got good at anything else. Is there something you wish you'd learned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Welding, maybe. My grandad welded everything on his farm, gates, trailers. Even a robot breaks, and someone has to fix the gate. I don't know if I'd actually do it, but I think about it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the country to make a plan and hope it gets on with it. I wouldn't march about something ten years off.
S4.think: My boss will likely have retired by then anyway, so my job was always going to change. What worries me is being thirty-seven with no real trade, and my partner the same.
S4.do: Keeps working at the hill farm while her boss is there and keeps saving. Puts off the mortgage she and her partner planned for next year and keeps renting, doing little else until she has to.
S4.feel: A slow anxiety that sits under everything.
S4.quote: Even a robot breaks, and someone has to fix the gate.
S4.fieldNote: More time doesn't calm Nora much, because her deeper fear is lacking a trade, not the robots themselves. The one concrete change she'd make is delaying a mortgage, which she knows frustrates her partner. Welding came up as a wish, not a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Luc and I would both be out at once and I'm not quick enough to land somewhere new. What would help is money to tide us over for a year, so we didn't have to give up the house. And someone telling me plainly what jobs are left, not a website, a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we'd still want to live out here. I think we would. Even with no work, I'd rather be skint on a hill than skint in a town. That's probably daft.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be skint on a hill than skint in a town.
portrait: Nora Moreau is a 27-year-old junior hand on Upper Banks, a hill beef farm run by a 66-year-old widower, Owen, where she feeds and beds cattle and still sometimes gets the feed mix wrong. She lives with Luc, a milk tanker driver, and they have about four months saved. She has never used AI and doesn't plan to, and she is honest that she would give younger people advice to learn new things that she won't take herself. She stays calm if nothing changes, uneasy with steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years because both incomes in her home could go at once. With more time, she expects to put things off, cut back and delay a mortgage.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her partner would both lose work at once and she isn't quick to find something new.
whatWouldHelp: A year's income to tide them over so they could keep their home, and a real person telling her plainly what jobs are left.
